title: RewardFlow: Can Action-Level Reward Be Estimated from State-Graph Topology in Agentic RL?
claim: Our method beats strong baselines across diverse tasks, matches costlier learned reward models, and adds negligible training overhead.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, bar charts, blue takeaway sentence under each
description: A wide row of three grouped bar charts, each with a bold title above and a blue takeaway sentence below. Panel (a) compares RewardFlow with RL baselines (Base, RLOO, GRPO, Search-R1, GiGPO) on success rate for ALFWorld, WebShop, Sokoban, plus single-hop and multi-hop search, separated by a dashed line. Panel (b) compares RewardFlow with GRPO and process reward models (ArmoRM-8B, Selene-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B, showing 62.8 against 50.0. Panel (c) shows average time per training step for ALFWorld, WebShop and Sokoban, with a broken y-axis. It stacks sample, update, ref and old-policy costs, and RewardFlow computation is only 1.5 to 2.4 s. Baselines are in grey shades. RewardFlow is highlighted with blue diagonal hatching and bold value labels.
caption: RewardFlow improves agent learning. (a) Averaged across evaluated model scales, RewardFlow achieves higher success rates on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban and higher search accuracy than the RL baselines. (b) On ALFWorld, Qwen2.5-1.5B trained with RewardFlow achieves a 62.8% success rate, compared with 50.0% for GRPO and 48.4% for GRPO with Selene-8B, the strongest evaluated PRM baseline. (c) Graph construction and reward estimation take 1.47-2.39 s per training step, using Qwen2.5-3B on ALFWorld and WebShop and Qwen2.5-VL-3B on Sokoban.
abstract: In agentic tasks such as household assistance and web shopping, large language model (LLM) agents take multiple actions before receiving a final outcome indicating success or failure. For reinforcement learning (RL), this outcome obscures individual actions' contributions: a shopping trajectory may find the right product but fail to complete the purchase. To address this credit-assignment problem, we introduce RewardFlow, which connects multiple trajectories for the same task through shared states (states grouped by task-relevant equivalence or semantic similarity). The resulting directed state graph links observed trajectory segments. Therefore, an action in a failed trajectory may reach a state from which another trajectory succeeds. It propagates reward signals backward from states where the task succeeds, assigning state potentials that decrease with shortest-path distance to success in the graph. Potential differences then reward actions that reduce this distance, bringing the agent closer to success in the graph. These estimated rewards yield action-level advantages that complement trajectory-level advantages from outcome rewards during policy optimization, without a learned process reward model or manual action-level annotations. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, Sokoban, and search tasks show gains over RL baselines across model scales. With 3B policies, graph construction and reward estimation take $1.47$-$2.39$ seconds per training step on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban (Fig. 1). Code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/RewardFlow.
